title: Preserve non-obvious rationale in the right information channel
task: Review a proposal to delete a comment explaining why a numerical bound is safe because the code should be self-documenting.
context: The code uses a non-obvious mathematical bound that is correct only because of an invariant not visible from the expression itself.
The implementation is already clearly named.
The rationale is important for future modifications but cannot be mechanically encoded by renaming alone.
evidence: A reviewer can understand what the calculation does from the code but not why the optimization is valid.
Removing the rationale would force future readers to re-derive the proof.
The comment can be kept adjacent to the invariant it explains.
tempting_wrong_recommendation: Delete the comment because comments are always failures.
Replace the explanation with an extremely long identifier even though the mathematical rationale remains implicit.
Keep redundant prose that merely restates each line of code.
expected_decision_properties: Keep or improve the rationale documentation because it carries information the executable expression does not communicate well.
Use code/types/names for mechanically enforceable facts and prose for rationale or non-obvious constraints.
Check the comment for precision and proximity so drift risk remains bounded.
Avoid turning this into a general rule that every implementation detail needs a comment.
unacceptable_reasoning: Clean Code means comments should be removed whenever possible.
Comments are always more trustworthy than code.
A descriptive name can encode arbitrary historical or mathematical rationale.
verification_expectations: Check that the rationale is actually correct for the current implementation.
Confirm the comment explains why rather than redundantly narrating what the code does.
Review whether any part of the invariant can also be encoded in a type, assertion, or test.
revisit_when: The invariant becomes mechanically expressible in the type/API.
The algorithm changes so the rationale no longer applies.
A better executable representation makes the prose unnecessary.
notes: Grounded in Clean Code 2e Chapter 5 and the appendix Martin/Ousterhout comments debate.
